target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection provides unique hands-on learning, career inspiration, and productive use of animals already dead.
objection: Dissection should not be required because the same educational goals can be met equally well or better with modern alternatives such as synthetic models, preserved specimens, and computer simulations, and the animals used are typically obtained in inhumane, environmentally harmful ways that outweigh the classroom benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that most dissection animals are already-dead byproducts and that sourcing concerns are overstated.
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, dissection still depends on killing animals for classroom use, so it is not a reliable ethical substitute for doing no harm; byproduct-only sourcing also cannot justify making dissection a standard requirement when alternatives exist.

target: AG1’s argument that students can simply opt out while others benefit from dissection.
objection: An opt-out policy does not solve the ethical problem because it still pressures objecting students to handle dead animals or lose instructional time and full curriculum access, creating coercion and exclusion that are unnecessary when standards-based learning can be met with alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that opting out and using humane sourcing makes dissection acceptable as a classroom option.
objection: Opt-out does not remove the core harm because schools still purchase and prepare animals, sustaining demand; and humane sourcing cannot be assumed to make dissection acceptable when the broader pattern is still wild-capture and biodiversity loss.

target: AG1’s claim that opt-out plus byproduct sourcing reduces the ethical problem to a manageable classroom policy issue.
objection: Opt-out still leaves students who object disadvantaged in practice, and byproduct sourcing does not eliminate the underlying ethical and environmental harm or the upstream supply-chain effects of classroom demand for animal remains.

target: AG1’s claim that banning dissection may not eliminate animal death because alternatives can still use animal-derived materials.
objection: The existence of some animal-derived alternatives elsewhere does not justify dissection; schools can choose non-animal options that meet the same concepts without acquiring animals’ bodies, and dissection adds environmental and safety burdens such as biohazards, disposal, and chemical use.

target: AG1’s ‘waste vs. use’ argument that using food-industry animal bodies for dissection is a responsible way to extract educational value from something already being discarded.
objection: Using animal bodies for class still creates extra demand for those tissues and can incentivize more animals to be bred, raised, caught, or processed; it does not meaningfully offset harm, and the claim that the specimens were ‘already going to be discarded’ cannot be reliably verified.

target: AG1’s claim that fetal pigs and similar specimens are already dead byproducts, so dissection does not create new killings and teaches unique real-world variability.
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, the ethical issue is still the use of dead sentient animals as teaching consumables, which is unnecessary when non-lethal methods can teach the same biology; moreover, schools cannot guarantee that every specimen truly comes from byproduct-only channels.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is not required by standards but is still a valuable, high-impact learning method that can be ethically regulated through procurement and accommodations.
objection: Dissection is not ethically necessary because comparable learning can be achieved with non-animal, hands-on alternatives, and requiring animal dissection still normalizes using dead sentient animals when curriculum goals can be met without that harm.

target: AG1’s claim that ‘true parity’ opt-out arrangements can make dissection fair and ethically acceptable for students who choose it.
objection: Even a parity model does not solve the central ethical problem that biology classes do not need carcass dissection at all; it also adds logistical burdens that may not be implemented consistently, so the safest policy is to avoid dissection-based demand altogether.

target: AG1’s claim that, with humane sourcing and respect-and-care framing, dissection can be an ethical educational compromise.
objection: The moral problem is not just sourcing but the fact that dissection still uses dead animals as consumable teaching material when the curriculum can be met without it; a respectful framing cannot erase that underlying avoidable harm.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches real lab science skills such as equipment setup, careful cuts, observation, safety, and disposal.
objection: Those procedural and safety skills do not require carcass dissection; schools can teach the same core competencies with non-animal lab work, synthetic models, prepared specimens, and other hands-on biology activities that avoid dismembering vertebrates.

target: AG1’s claim that high-quality alternatives may be too expensive or difficult for some schools, so dissection should remain available to preserve hands-on learning.
objection: Cost and implementation constraints do not justify using animals when dissection is not required by standards; the ethical response is to fund and design non-animal labs rather than keep carcass-based dissection as the default.
